examples.question_text: Find the general primitive of $f'(x)=(4x+3)^3$, then check your answer by differentiating.
examples.solution_text:
Increase the power by $1$ and divide by the new power and the coefficient of $x$.
$\begin{align*}f(x)&=\frac{(4x+3)^4}{4(4)}+C\\&=\frac{(4x+3)^4}{16}+C\end{align*}$
Check using the chain rule:
$\begin{align*}\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{(4x+3)^4}{16}+C\right)&=\frac{4(4x+3)^3\times4}{16}\\&=(4x+3)^3\end{align*}$

Keep the multiplier $14$, then divide by the new power and the coefficient of $x$.
$\begin{align*}f(x)&=\frac{14(2x+5)^7}{2(7)}+C\\&=(2x+5)^7+C\end{align*}$

examples.question_text: Find the general primitive of $f'(x)=\frac{8}{(5-2x)^3}$, writing your answer without a negative index.
examples.solution_text:
Rewrite the denominator using a negative index.
$\begin{align*}f'(x)&=\frac{8}{(5-2x)^3}\\&=8(5-2x)^{-3}\end{align*}$
The new power is $-2$ and the coefficient of $x$ is $-2$.
$\begin{align*}f(x)&=\frac{8(5-2x)^{-2}}{(-2)(-2)}+C\\&=2(5-2x)^{-2}+C\\&=\frac{2}{(5-2x)^2}+C\end{align*}$

(a) Rewrite the square root using a fractional index.
$\begin{align*}f'(x)&=(2-5x)^{\frac12}\\f(x)&=\frac{(2-5x)^{\frac32}}{-5\left(\frac32\right)}+C\\&=-\frac{2(2-5x)^{\frac32}}{15}+C\end{align*}$
(b) A square root in the denominator gives an index of $-\frac12$.
$\begin{align*}g'(x)&=4(2x+3)^{-\frac12}\\g(x)&=\frac{4(2x+3)^{\frac12}}{2\left(\frac12\right)}+C\\&=4\sqrt{2x+3}+C\end{align*}$
(c) Rewrite the cube root using an index of $\frac23$.
$\begin{align*}h'(x)&=(3x+4)^{\frac23}\\h(x)&=\frac{(3x+4)^{\frac53}}{3\left(\frac53\right)}+C\\&=\frac{(3x+4)^{\frac53}}{5}+C\end{align*}$

Questions and solutions remain separate editable fields; solution prose and mathematics inherit renderer blue. Relation signs are aligned, with no bare opening expressions requiring phantom gutters. These algebraic examples need no diagrams. Practice and quiz mathematics were neither altered nor re-audited. Independent review of the new examples and actual rendering verification remain pending.

examples.derivation: For a=4 and n=3, the primitive is (4x+3)^4/[4(4)]+C=(4x+3)^4/16+C. Differentiating gives 4(4x+3)^3·4/16=(4x+3)^3. This follows the bracket-power rule and differentiation check taught at source lines 354–361 and 395–410.
For a=-3 and n=5, the primitive is (7-3x)^6/[(-3)(6)]+C=-(7-3x)^6/18+C. Its derivative is (-1/18)·6·(-3)(7-3x)^5=(7-3x)^5. The signed-coefficient method matches source lines 395–420 and 435–437.

Retaining the multiplier gives 14(2x+5)^7/[2(7)]+C=(2x+5)^7+C. Differentiation gives 7·2(2x+5)^6=14(2x+5)^6. This combines the constant-multiple rule at source lines 195–203 with the linear-bracket rule and source exercises at lines 439–441.

Rewrite 8/(5-2x)^3 as 8(5-2x)^(-3). The primitive is 8(5-2x)^(-2)/[(-2)(-2)]+C=2/(5-2x)^2+C. Differentiation gives 2·(-2)·(-2)(5-2x)^(-3)=8/(5-2x)^3, on either interval excluding x=5/2. The rewrite and positive-index answer match source lines 284–291 and 439–441.

(a) With a=-5 and n=1/2, division by (-5)(3/2) gives -2(2-5x)^(3/2)/15+C; differentiation recovers sqrt(2-5x). (b) Rewrite as 4(2x+3)^(-1/2); division by 2(1/2) gives 4sqrt(2x+3)+C, whose derivative is 4/sqrt(2x+3). (c) Rewrite the cube root as (3x+4)^(2/3); division by 3(5/3) gives (3x+4)^(5/3)/5+C. Its derivative recovers the integrand, including derivative zero at x=-4/3 under the real cube-root interpretation. These combine the fractional-index teaching at source lines 294–300 and 313–319 with the bracket-root example at lines 402–412.
